name: EBCI Bean and Hominy
region: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians / Indigenous Americas
imageAlt: Illustrative bowl of prepared hominy maize, the defining corn ingredient in this EBCI bean-and-hominy recipe
imageCredit: Photo: Glane23, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Ingredient image; not a photograph of the finished EBCI dish.
summary: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Bean and Hominy with hulled corn, kidney beans and lean salt pork, adapted from Nakoa Chiltoske’s Tribal Foods recipe.
lead: Prepared hominy corn, beans and a modest amount of salt pork simmer together in a Cherokee community recipe published by EBCI Tribal Foods.
about: The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods program publishes Bean and Hominy by Nakoa Chiltoske as a short, practical recipe built from dried hominy corn, kidney beans, lean salt pork and water. The community source also documents the traditional possibility of hickory ash during corn preparation, while allowing baking soda as a practical alternative.
story: Corn and beans have long relationships within Cherokee foodways, but this page stays specifically with the modern community recipe that EBCI chose to publish. The Tribal Foods instructions include dehulling corn after alkaline treatment and cooking beans with lean salt pork before combining them. Because ash processing carries practical safety considerations, this adaptation recommends beginning with food-ready hominy unless the cook is already working from community-grounded instruction.
caveat: This page is an adaptation of a recipe publicly shared by Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods. For home safety and simplicity, the method below starts with dried food-ready hominy rather than teaching improvised hardwood-ash processing.
prepNotes: Start with food-ready hominy
If you do not already know community-grounded ash processing, buy dried hominy that is already hulled and ready for cooking.
Soak corn and beans separately
Their hydration and cook times can differ, so separate soaking gives better control.
Salt late
Salt pork contributes substantial salinity; taste the combined pot before adding any extra salt.
ingredients: 2 cups dried food-ready hominy, soaked overnight and drained
1 cup dried kidney beans, soaked overnight and drained
6 oz lean salt pork, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
8 cups water, plus more as needed
steps: Place soaked hominy in a heavy pot and cover with fresh water by about 2 inches. Bring to a boil, reduce to a simmer and cook 60–90 minutes until the kernels are becoming tender.
In a second pot combine soaked kidney beans, salt pork and enough water to cover by 2 inches. Simmer 45–60 minutes until beans are nearly tender.
Drain excess liquid from the hominy only if necessary, then combine corn with the beans, pork and enough bean broth to make a moist, spoonable dish.
Simmer together 30 minutes over low heat.
Checkpoint: hominy should be plump and tender but not disintegrating, beans creamy inside and pork fully cooked and soft.
Taste before seasoning. Add black pepper if desired and extra salt only if the pork has not already seasoned the pot sufficiently.
Serve hot as a substantial corn-and-bean dish.
sources: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Bean and Hominy by Nakoa Chiltoske
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Cherokee Foodways

name: Ethiopian Azifa
imageAlt: Illustrative green lentils, the defining ingredient in Ethiopian azifa
imageCredit: Wikimedia Commons image of green lentils; ingredient image used because a reliably licensed exact azifa photograph was not verified.
summary: Ethiopian azifa: cool green lentils tossed with red onion, jalapeño, mustard, lemon and olive oil for a bright counterpoint to richer wots.
lead: Lentils move out of the stew pot and into a cool, lemony salad sharpened with mustard, onion and fresh chile.
about: Azifa is an Ethiopian lentil salad usually served cool or at room temperature. Green or brown lentils hold their shape, while red onion, chile, lemon or lime and ground mustard create a sharp dressing. Some versions lightly mash part of the lentils for a creamier texture while leaving enough whole for bite.
story: Ethiopian cook Eleni Woldeyes describes azifa as a refreshing cold lentil salad often shared at family gatherings and potlucks, with brown mustard seed providing a particularly characteristic flavor. Published Ethiopian recipes differ in ginger, turmeric, tomato and whether onion and chile are raw or briefly sautéed. Its bright acidity makes it especially useful beside richer lentil, meat and vegetable dishes on an injera spread.
caveat: Azifa formulas vary. This version keeps the lentils mostly whole and uses mustard, lemon, onion and jalapeño as the central flavoring; households may make it smoother or include additional aromatics.
prepNotes: Use green or brown lentils
Red lentils collapse too easily for the salad texture used here.
Stop before mushy
Drain as soon as lentils are tender all the way through but still hold their shape.
Dress while barely warm
Slight warmth helps the lentils absorb seasoning, then chilling settles the flavors.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups dried green or brown lentils, rinsed
1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Combine lentils and water in a saucepan, bring to a boil and simmer uncovered 20–30 minutes.
Checkpoint: lentils should be tender at the center but retain distinct skins and shapes. Drain thoroughly.
Whisk lemon juice, olive oil, mustard and salt in a serving bowl.
Add warm lentils and toss. Let cool 10 minutes.
Fold in red onion, jalapeño and parsley if using. Lightly mash 1/4 cup lentils against the bowl if you want a slightly creamier dressing.
Chill 20–30 minutes or serve at room temperature.
Taste again for lemon, mustard and salt before serving with injera or as part of a larger Ethiopian spread.
sources: Eleni's Kitchen — Ethiopian Azifa Lentil Salad

name: Nigerian Akara
imageCredit: Photo: Linason Blessing, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Nigerian akara: peeled black-eyed peas whipped with onion and chile, then fried into crisp bean cakes with airy, tender centers.
lead: Black-eyed peas become breakfast when they are peeled, ground, aerated and dropped into hot oil as crisp-edged akara.
about: Akara are West African bean fritters, especially familiar in Nigeria as breakfast or street food. Peeled black-eyed peas are ground with onion and chile, then the batter is whipped to trap air before frying. Good akara are crisp outside and remarkably light inside rather than dense bean paste.
story: Nigerian food photography and culinary sources consistently identify akara as a staple breakfast and street snack. Food Network’s Nigerian Dinner episode features a recipe by Simbo Fowora built from soaked peeled black-eyed peas, onion and red pepper. Closely related bean fritters exist across West Africa under names including koose, and the tradition also traveled across the Atlantic, where it became part of Afro-Brazilian acarajé culture.
caveat: Akara seasoning and texture differ by household and region. This Nigerian version uses black-eyed peas, onion and fresh chile and does not attempt to merge Nigerian akara with Brazilian acarajé serving traditions.
prepNotes: Peel the beans
Removing the skins makes the interior much lighter; rubbing soaked beans between your palms helps loosen them.
Keep batter thick
Too much blender water makes the fritters absorb oil and spread.
Whip before frying
Several minutes of beating incorporates air and is one of the keys to a fluffy center.
ingredients: 2 cups dried black-eyed peas, soaked overnight
1 red bell pepper or 2 red chiles, chopped
1/4 cup water, approximately, only as needed for blending
Neutral or palm oil, for frying
steps: Drain soaked peas and rub handfuls vigorously between your palms in water to loosen skins. Skim away floating skins and repeat until most are removed.
Blend peeled peas with onion and peppers, adding only enough water for the blades to move. The batter should be thick and spoonable.
Transfer to a bowl, add salt and beat vigorously with a whisk or wooden spoon for 3–5 minutes.
Checkpoint: batter should look slightly lighter and fluffier and a spoonful should hold a mound rather than run flat.
Heat 2 inches oil to 350–360°F. Drop rounded tablespoons of batter into the oil without crowding.
Fry 3–5 minutes, turning, until deep golden brown.
Checkpoint: fritters should feel crisp outside and split open to an airy, fully cooked bean interior with no wet paste.
Drain and serve hot with pap/ogi, bread or a fresh pepper sauce.
sources: Food Network — Akara by Simbo Fowora, Nigerian Dinner
Wikimedia Commons — Nigerian Akara cultural photography

name: Puerto Rican Mofongo
imageAlt: Puerto Rican mofongo made from fried green plantains
imageCredit: Photo: Diane, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY 2.0
summary: Puerto Rican mofongo with twice-fried green plantain mashed with garlic, olive oil and chicharrón into a savory mound ready for broth, meat or seafood.
lead: Fried green plantain, garlic and crisp pork are pounded together while hot—the action that gives mofongo its unmistakable dense, savory texture.
about: Mofongo is a Puerto Rican plantain dish made by frying green plantain pieces and pounding them with garlic, fat and usually chicharrón. It may be shaped into a mound, filled with meat or seafood or served with broth alongside. The texture should be cohesive and rustic, with small plantain pieces still perceptible rather than a smooth purée.
story: Discover Puerto Rico treats mofongo as an essential island food and publishes chef Mario Pagán’s green-plantain method. The dish reflects Puerto Rico’s layered culinary history: plantains arrived through African and Atlantic foodways, while pounding methods and garlic seasoning evolved locally. Mofongo today ranges from humble side dish to elaborate restaurant centerpiece stuffed with seafood or meat.
caveat: Puerto Rican cooks vary the fat, garlic, broth and filling. This version focuses on the classic green-plantain-and-chicharrón base rather than a restaurant-style stuffed presentation.
prepNotes: Use green plantains
Yellow ripe plantains are sweet and too soft for classic mofongo.
Pound while hot
Warm fried plantain binds much more readily with garlic and pork fat.
Do not over-purée
Mofongo should be cohesive but still rustic and slightly chunky.
ingredients: 1 cup crushed chicharrón or crisp bacon
1/3 to 1/2 cup warm chicken broth, as needed
Broth, meat or seafood, optional for serving
steps: Peel green plantains and cut into 1-inch rounds. Soak in lightly salted water 15 minutes, then dry thoroughly.
Heat 1 1/2 inches neutral oil to 325–340°F. Fry plantain pieces 5–7 minutes until tender and lightly golden rather than crisp brown.
Pound garlic and salt in a mortar until pasty. Add olive oil and chicharrón and crush together.
Add hot fried plantains in batches and pound, folding the mixture between additions.
Checkpoint: the mixture should hold together when pressed but retain small irregular pieces of plantain and pork rather than becoming baby-food smooth.
Work in warm broth a tablespoon at a time only if the mofongo is too dry to bind.
Pack into small bowls or shape by hand and invert onto plates. Serve immediately, optionally with broth or a meat or seafood topping.
sources: Discover Puerto Rico — Chef Mario Pagán's Mofongo
Discover Puerto Rico — Mofongo and Puerto Rican cuisine

name: Uzbek Manti
imageAlt: Uzbek manti steamed dumplings filled with meat
imageCredit: Photo: Sfbarb, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Uzbek manti with very thin dough wrapped around a juicy lamb-and-onion filling and steamed in tiers until tender.
lead: Thin dough and an unusually juicy onion-rich meat filling meet steam—not boiling water—in Uzbekistan’s large manti dumplings.
about: Uzbek manti are large steamed dumplings filled with finely chopped or minced meat and onion, often with lamb fat for succulence. Uzbekistan’s official tourism site emphasizes two technical rules: the dough should be very thin, around 2 millimeters, and the filling should stay juicy. The dumplings steam in a multi-tier mantovarka rather than boil.
story: Manti belong to a broad Central Asian and Turkic dumpling family with many local forms. Uzbekistan Travel documents meat, pumpkin, fried, broth-cooked and other variations and notes suzma or chakka as a common accompaniment. This page stays with the familiar steamed lamb-and-onion form while recognizing that Uzbek manti are not one immutable shape or filling.
caveat: Manti vary across Uzbekistan and neighboring Central Asian cultures. This recipe is specifically framed as an Uzbek steamed meat manti and does not collapse those neighboring traditions together.
prepNotes: Chop onion generously
Onion supplies moisture to the filling; the ratio can look surprisingly high before cooking.
Keep dough thin but strong
About 2 mm is the target—thin enough to be delicate, sturdy enough to hold broth.
Oil the steamer
A light film prevents the bottoms from welding themselves to the basket.
ingredients: 1 lb ground or finely chopped lamb
3 oz lamb fat or 2 tbsp butter, finely diced, optional
Plain yogurt or suzma, for serving
steps: Mix flour and salt. Add egg and water gradually and knead 8–10 minutes into a firm smooth dough. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
Mix lamb, onions, lamb fat if using, cumin, pepper and filling salt. Chill while rolling dough.
Roll dough to about 2 mm thick and cut into 4-inch squares.
Place a heaping tablespoon filling in the center of each square and seal by bringing opposite corners together, then pinching adjacent edges into the preferred manti shape.
Lightly oil steamer trays and arrange manti with space between them.
Steam over actively boiling water 35–40 minutes.
Checkpoint: wrappers should be tender and slightly translucent at thin edges, and filling must be fully cooked with hot juices inside.
Serve immediately with suzma, yogurt or butter and black pepper.
sources: Uzbekistan Travel — Manti, a Delicious Steamed Dumpling
Fringe Table — Caucasus, Central & West Asia food guide

name: Assamese Khar with Raw Papaya
imageAlt: An Assamese khar preparation; photographed version uses bamboo shoot while this home recipe uses raw papaya
imageCredit: Photo: Suditree, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. The photographed khar uses bamboo shoot; the page recipe uses raw papaya and labels that difference explicitly.
summary: Assamese raw-papaya khar using a carefully measured alkaline khar liquid to produce the clean, distinctive first course of an Assamese meal.
lead: Raw papaya meets the alkaline seasoning that is so characteristic of Assamese cooking that a traditional meal often begins with khar.
about: Khar is both an Assamese alkaline ingredient and the category of dishes prepared with it. Assam Tourism describes kola khar as liquid filtered through ashes of banana stem or peel and notes that khar dishes traditionally begin a meal. Raw papaya is one classic partner, though vegetables, pulses and fish can all appear in khar preparations.
story: Assam Tourism calls khar integral enough to Assamese cuisine that the phrase Khar Khuwa Asomiya—roughly, khar-eating Assamese—is used culturally. Its alkaline cooking medium is historically produced from banana-plant ash. Because home ash chemistry can vary unpredictably, this recipe does not ask unfamiliar cooks to improvise ash lye; it recommends a commercially prepared food-grade kola khar or a carefully measured baking-soda fallback while clearly noting that the substitute changes the result.
caveat: Do not improvise concentrated ash lye without experienced, food-specific guidance. Food-grade kola khar is preferred. A tiny amount of baking soda is only a practical substitute and is not culturally or chemically identical.
prepNotes: Use green raw papaya
Ripe fruit is too sweet and soft for this savory preparation.
Measure alkalinity cautiously
More khar is not better; excess creates harsh soapiness.
Do not chase health claims
Assam Tourism records traditional beliefs about khar, but this page presents it as food, not medicine.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb green raw papaya, peeled, seeded and cut into 1-inch pieces
1 to 2 tsp food-grade kola khar, to taste, or no more than 1/8 tsp baking soda as a fallback
3/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Heat mustard oil in a saucepan until shimmering. Add mustard seeds and dried chile and let the seeds crackle.
Add papaya and turmeric and toss 2 minutes.
Add water and salt, cover and simmer 15–18 minutes until papaya is nearly tender.
Stir in 1 teaspoon food-grade kola khar and simmer uncovered 3 minutes. If using the baking-soda fallback, use only 1/8 teaspoon.
Checkpoint: papaya should be soft but intact and the broth should have a subtle characteristic alkaline edge, never a strong soapy taste.
Taste before adding any additional kola khar. Reduce any excess liquid to a light coating consistency.
Serve warm near the beginning of an Assamese-style meal.
sources: Assam Tourism — Khar in Assamese Cuisine
Fringe Table — Himalayas & South Asia food guide

name: Betawi Gado-Gado
imageAlt: Indonesian gado-gado with vegetables and peanut sauce
imageCredit: Photo: Supardisahabu, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Betawi gado-gado with blanched vegetables, tofu, tempeh, potato and egg covered in a thick sweet-savory peanut sauce.
lead: A Jakarta plate of vegetables, tofu, tempeh and egg becomes gado-gado when everything disappears under a freshly ground peanut dressing.
about: Gado-gado is an Indonesian vegetable dish with strong Javanese and Betawi associations. Indonesia’s official tourism site specifically presents Gado-Gado Betawi as a Jakarta specialty combining vegetables with thick peanut sauce, ketupat, tofu and tempeh. Eggs and crackers are also common additions.
story: Indonesia Travel uses gado-gado as an example of Jakarta’s diverse Betawi food culture, describing many ingredients brought together on one plate. The vegetables are generally cooked separately so each retains its own texture, while the peanut sauce binds the meal. Rather than labeling every Indonesian peanut-dressed vegetable plate identically, this recipe follows the Betawi/Jakarta framing supplied by the national tourism authority.
caveat: Gado-gado varies around Java and Indonesia. This version is explicitly Betawi/Jakarta-style and should not be treated as the only legitimate regional form.
prepNotes: Cook vegetables separately
Beans, cabbage and sprouts need different times; separate blanching keeps them from all becoming equally soft.
Use fried tofu and tempeh
Their browned surfaces hold peanut sauce much better than plain steamed pieces.
Make sauce thick
Gado-gado dressing should cling heavily to the ingredients, not run like vinaigrette.
ingredients: 8 oz firm tofu, fried or pan-browned and cubed
Fried shallots and crackers, for serving
steps: Blanch cabbage, green beans and bean sprouts separately until just tender, cooling each promptly so they retain texture.
Arrange cooked vegetables, potatoes, tofu, tempeh, eggs and cucumber on a large platter.
Grind peanuts, garlic and chiles in a mortar or food processor until very fine but not completely smooth.
Add sugar, tamarind, kecap manis and salt. Work in hot water gradually.
Checkpoint: the sauce should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily and mound over vegetables rather than pour like broth.
Taste for sweet, sour, salty and chile balance.
Spoon sauce generously over the arranged ingredients and finish with fried shallots and crackers. Serve immediately.
sources: Fringe Table — Southeast Asia food guide
